strengths: The paper addresses a timely, underexplored problem: evaluating whether multimodal models can judge visualization quality beyond conventional chart question answering.

VISJUDGE-BENCH has useful breadth, with 3,090 real-world images spanning single visualizations, multi-view compositions, dashboards, and 32 reported subtypes. The six-dimensional annotations could support valuable diagnostic research.

The empirical study includes several recent open and proprietary MLLMs, per-dimension and per-visualization-type results, score-distribution analyses, and qualitative error cases. VISJUDGE shows substantial held-out improvement over its Qwen2.5-VL-7B base model and the evaluated general-purpose models.
The appendix documents the rubrics, prompts, data distribution, quality-control heuristics, reward function, and major training hyperparameters in considerable detail.
weaknesses: The central construct is not validly measured. Annotators receive rendered images and generated descriptions but no underlying data or chart specification, so they generally cannot determine whether a visualization faithfully represents its source data. The fidelity rubric instead conflates truthfulness with visible axes, labels, baselines, and internal consistency. Consequently, the headline claim of jointly measuring fidelity, expressiveness, and aesthetics is unsupported.

The claimed expert ground truth lacks essential reliability evidence. No inter-annotator agreement, expert agreement, split-half reliability, confidence intervals, or human performance ceiling is reported, despite the paper saying an agreement analysis was enabled. Initial annotators are broadly screened crowdworkers rather than demonstrated visualization experts; expert qualifications, independent scoring protocol, aggregation procedure, and the effects of modifying 58% of scores remain unclear.

GPT-4o-generated descriptions and sample-specific rubrics are neither validated nor ablated. They may contain hallucinations, prime annotators toward particular judgments, change the meaning of the scale across samples, and give models privileged textual interpretations of the image. Using GPT-4o both in benchmark construction and as an evaluated baseline further complicates interpretation.

The VISJUDGE comparison does not isolate the proposed training method: a task-trained model is compared primarily with zero-shot general models, without supervised fine-tuning, regression, calibration, category-mean, or retrieval baselines. There is no ablation of GRPO, LoRA, adaptive questions, individual reward terms, rationales, or dataset components. Rationales are rewarded only for being present and are evaluated only through selected examples.

The statistical evaluation is insufficient. Results lack repeated training seeds, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. Pearson correlation and MAE alone are limited for ordinal ratings. The overall score averages six subdimensions, implicitly weighting Aesthetics three times as much as Fidelity, while averaging can conceal offsetting subdimension errors. VISJUDGE's overall correlation of 0.681 exceeds every reported category-specific correlation (0.577, 0.565, and 0.375), suggesting that category-level score differences contribute substantially; no category-only baseline is provided.

Several results and claims are internally inconsistent. Table 3 makes Fidelity the worst baseline subdimension by average MAE, contradicting the text's claim that models perform relatively well on it. The stated 70/10/20 split counts of 2,163/279/648 correspond approximately to 70/9/21, and the scaling experiment uses 2,442 samples without reconciling this with the stated 2,163-sample training set. The abstract reports correlation improvement against GPT-5 although GPT-4o is the stronger correlation baseline, and 'scaling laws' are claimed from a small single-run study with only moderate correlation fit.

Dataset validity and generalization are insufficiently controlled. Quality-modified web-search queries can induce collection artifacts; image-level random splitting does not rule out leakage among templates, websites, or chart families; public web images may occur in model pretraining; and some advertised subtypes contain only one to three examples. No source-held-out, template-held-out, external-dataset, or accessibility/cultural generalization evaluation is provided.

Reproducibility and ethics are incomplete. The promised benchmark URL is blank, and no dataset, code, trained model, exact proprietary model versions, API dates, seeds, or image preprocessing settings are supplied. The statement that all inference used vLLM on local A6000 GPUs cannot describe GPT, Claude, and Gemini evaluation. Copyright compliance for crawled images is asserted without provenance or licensing procedures, while participant consent or research-ethics review is not discussed.
